specPoints.text: write word equations and balanced chemical equations(including state symbols):for reactions studied in this specificationfor unfamiliar reactions where suitable information is provided.

primer.text: You already know from Atomic Structure that matter is built from atoms, and that substances have names and formulae that say what is joined to what. This note turns that knowledge into the language of reactions: the word equation that describes change in names, and the balanced symbol equation that carries state symbols and exact atom counts.

lessons.title: Conservation of mass
lessons.opening: A chemical reaction makes new substances, yet no atom disappears: every atom present before the change is still there afterwards, only joined up in different ways. Mass is therefore never lost. That principle is the Law of Conservation of Mass, and it is what allows a chemical equation to balance at all.
keyPoints: New substances form in a reaction, but the same atoms are present before and after.
Atoms cannot be created or destroyed, so every atom in the reactants must appear in the products.
The total mass of the reactants always equals the total mass of the products.
This principle is the Law of Conservation of Mass, and it is what makes balancing possible.

low.restatement: Nothing disappears in a reaction. Every atom you start with is still there at the end, so the mass you can weigh before equals the mass you can weigh after.
low.analogy: A set of building bricks: snap a model apart and rebuild it in a new shape — every brick is still on the table, so nothing is lost or gained.
low.examPointer: When a question asks why mass is conserved, answer that atoms are neither created nor destroyed — never merely that the equation was balanced.

medium.restatement: The Law of Conservation of Mass states that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, so the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products in every chemical change.
medium.analogy: A closed workshop: raw material goes in, finished goods come out, and nothing vanishes between the two — only how the pieces are joined together changes.
medium.examPointer: Conservation of mass underpins every balancing task in this note; state the law explicitly when an answer asks you to justify why an equation can be balanced.

check.stem: 10.0 g of mercury(II) oxide is heated in a sealed container and decomposes completely into mercury and oxygen. What is the total mass of mercury and oxygen present afterwards?

options.explanation: The vessel is sealed, so every atom stays inside: the atoms of mercury(II) oxide have merely rearranged into mercury and oxygen.

options.text: Less than 10.0 g
options.explanation: A gas still has mass; nothing leaves a sealed container simply by becoming gaseous.
options.misconception: dismisses the mass of gaseous products

options.text: More than 10.0 g
options.explanation: Heating supplies energy, not atoms, so no extra mass can appear.
options.misconception: treats heating as adding mass

options.text: Cannot be told without weighing
options.explanation: Conservation of mass predicts the total exactly, so no new weighing is needed.
options.misconception: denies that conservation makes the mass predictable

check.stem: Which principle is the reason a chemical equation can be balanced at all?

options.text: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction
options.explanation: Balancing works because the same atoms must appear on both sides, only rearranged.

options.text: Mass depends on the volume a substance occupies
options.explanation: Volume changes as substances change state; it plays no part in why balancing is possible.
options.misconception: confuses conservation with volume arguments

options.text: Every reaction can run backwards as well as forwards
options.explanation: Reversibility is a separate idea; balancing does not depend on it.
options.misconception: imports reversibility as the justification

options.text: A catalyst changes the products of a reaction
options.explanation: A catalyst only alters the rate; it neither appears in the balanced result nor justifies balancing.
options.misconception: overstates what a catalyst does

check.stem: In a sealed vessel, 71 g of chlorine is supplied and 23 g of sodium reacts completely, leaving 35.5 g of chlorine unreacted. What mass of sodium chloride has formed?

options.explanation: Total mass is conserved: 23 + 71 = 94 g before, and 94 − 35.5 = 58.5 g of chlorine remains, so 58.5 g must be sodium chloride.
94 g is the total starting mass; it ignores the 35.5 g of chlorine left over.
options.misconception: ignores the unreacted excess when closing the mass account

options.explanation: 35.5 g is the leftover chlorine, not the product that formed.
options.misconception: reports the leftover reactant as the product

options.explanation: The product contains atoms from both reactants, so its mass must exceed the sodium's alone.
options.misconception: counts only one reactant's mass in the product

check.stem: A candle burns inside an open jar, and the jar's contents weigh less afterwards. Does this contradict the Law of Conservation of Mass?

options.text: No — gaseous products escaped from the jar into the air
options.explanation: The system is open, so the missing mass left as gases; conservation applies to the candle plus the air taken together.

options.text: Yes — the contents lost mass, and mass can never change
options.explanation: The law compares total mass including escaped gases, not just what remains in the jar.
options.misconception: applies conservation to an open system's visible contents only

options.text: Yes — burning destroys some of the atoms
options.explanation: Burning rearranges atoms; it never destroys them.
options.misconception: believes combustion destroys matter

options.text: No — solids always weigh less after heating
options.explanation: The conclusion happens to be no, but the reasoning is wrong: the mass left as gases is the true reason.
options.misconception: reaches the right verdict through an invented rule

check.stem: Spec point 1.25 asks you to write word and balanced chemical equations. For which reactions does this apply?

options.text: Reactions studied in the specification and unfamiliar ones where suitable information is provided
options.explanation: Both cases are named: the reactions you have met, and new ones you can interpret from the details supplied.

options.text: Only the reactions studied in the specification
options.explanation: The skill extends beyond the studied list to unfamiliar reactions with enough information given.
options.misconception: narrows the required scope to familiar reactions

options.text: Only unfamiliar reactions
options.explanation: Studied reactions remain firmly included; unfamiliar ones are an addition, not a replacement.
options.misconception: inverts the scope, dropping studied reactions

options.text: Only reactions where state symbols are demanded
options.explanation: State symbols are part of the equation format, not a limit on which reactions apply.
options.misconception: confuses the state-symbol requirement with the scope of the skill

lessons.title: How to write word equations
lessons.opening: A word equation describes a reaction in full names: reactants on the left, products on the right, an arrow between them read as to form. Sodium hydroxide reacting with hydrochloric acid becomes sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water. No formulae are needed yet — only the names, placed on the correct side of the arrow.
keyPoints: A word equation names the reactants on the left and the products on the right of an arrow.
The arrow is read as to form or produces and signals conversion of reactants into products.
A reaction condition or a catalyst's name may be written above the arrow.
Reactants are the chemical ingredients of the reaction, mixed together before it starts.

low.restatement: A word equation is a sentence about a reaction that uses full names: write the substances you start with, add an arrow, then write what they become.
low.analogy: Like a recipe line — flour + eggs → cake. The arrow is the oven: everything on its left turns into everything on its right.
low.examPointer: If a question names the products first, still put them on the right: the order words appear in the sentence is not the order of the equation.

medium.restatement: In a word equation the reactants sit on the left of the arrow and the products on the right; any reaction condition or catalyst sits above the arrow, which itself reads as to form.
medium.analogy: Treat it as a transformation sentence written in plain code: inputs on the left, outputs on the right, with the processing note — heat, catalyst — annotated on the arrow itself.
medium.examPointer: Multi-word questions hide the arrow in verbs such as forms, produces or reacts with; mark each substance as reactant or product before writing anything down.

check.stem: Sodium hydroxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form sodium chloride and water. Which word equation is correct?

options.text: sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water
options.explanation: The two starting substances sit left of the arrow and the two new substances sit right, exactly as the sentence states.

options.text: sodium chloride + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid
options.explanation: This reverses the reaction: the products named in the sentence have been written on the left.
options.misconception: writes the products where the reactants belong

options.text: sodium + chlorine → sodium chloride
options.explanation: The reactants are compounds with full names of their own; swapping in element names loses hydroxide and the acid.
options.misconception: substitutes element names for the actual reactants

options.text: sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water
options.explanation: Hydrochloric acid is a starting substance and must appear on the left; it has been dropped entirely.
options.misconception: omits a reactant from the equation

check.stem: Iron(II) hydroxide and sodium sulfate are formed when iron(II) sulfate solution and sodium hydroxide react together. Which word equation matches?

options.text: iron(II) sulfate + sodium hydroxide → iron(II) hydroxide + sodium sulfate
options.explanation: The substances that are formed are the products, so they belong on the right even though the sentence mentions them first.

options.text: iron(II) hydroxide + sodium sulfate → iron(II) sulfate + sodium hydroxide
options.explanation: This copies the mention order; the formed substances have been placed on the left by mistake.
options.misconception: copies the order of mention instead of the reaction direction

options.text: iron(II) sulfate + sodium hydroxide → iron(II) sulfate + sodium hydroxide
options.explanation: The right-hand side merely restates the starting substances; no new substances have been written.
options.misconception: restates the reactants as the products

options.text: iron(II) sulfate → iron(II) hydroxide + sodium sulfate
options.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is the second starting substance and must appear on the left.
options.misconception: drops a reactant while reading the sentence

check.stem: Coal is mainly carbon, and it burns in air. Which word equation describes the reaction?

options.text: carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Burning in air means reacting with oxygen, so oxygen is the second reactant.

options.text: carbon → carbon dioxide
options.explanation: The oxygen from the air is a reactant and must be named on the left.
options.misconception: omits oxygen when a substance burns in air

options.text: carbon + air → carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Air is the mixture the oxygen comes from; the reacting substance named in equations is oxygen.
options.misconception: names air, not oxygen, as the reactant

options.text: carbon dioxide → carbon + oxygen
options.explanation: This reverses the burning process, putting the products on the left.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the reaction

check.stem: In a word equation, what does the arrow represent?

options.text: The conversion of the reactants into the products
options.explanation: The arrow is read as to form or produces: the substances on the left become the substances on the right.

options.text: That both sides contain the same substances
options.explanation: Reactants and products are different substances; the arrow is not an equals sign.
options.misconception: reads the arrow as an equality of the two sides

options.text: That the reactants dissolve into each other
options.explanation: Dissolving is a physical change; the arrow describes a chemical reaction making new substances.
options.misconception: confuses the reaction arrow with dissolving

options.text: That heat is always needed for the reaction
options.explanation: Some reactions need heating and some do not; the bare arrow itself carries no such claim.
options.misconception: assumes every reaction is heated

check.stem: A reaction is speeded up using a catalyst. Where does the catalyst's name appear in the word equation?

options.text: Written above the arrow
options.explanation: A catalyst is neither consumed nor formed, so its name is annotated on the arrow itself.

options.text: On the left, as one of the reactants
options.explanation: Reactants are consumed; a catalyst is only added to make the reaction go faster and survives unchanged.
options.misconception: treats the catalyst as a consumed ingredient

options.text: On the right, as one of the products
options.explanation: Products are new substances made by the reaction; the catalyst is not one of them.
options.misconception: treats the catalyst as a formed substance

options.text: Nowhere — catalysts are never shown
options.explanation: The note is explicit: the catalyst's name can be written above the arrow.
options.misconception: denies that catalysts are annotated on equations

lessons.title: How to write balanced equations
lessons.opening: A symbol equation uses formulae instead of names, and it must balance: the same number of atoms of every element on both sides. Write the diatomic non-metals as molecules — H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, I2 — and add state symbols when they are asked for. Work left to right, one element at a time, and leave elements standing alone until last.
keyPoints: A symbol equation uses formulae, and it must show the correct ratio of reactants and products.
Write the non-metals H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2 as molecules.
State symbols are solid (s), liquid (l), gas (g) and aqueous (aq), and good practice keeps them in every equation.
Count an unchanged group such as the nitrate group as one entity instead of individual atoms.
Leave elements that stand alone until last when balancing.

low.restatement: Change only the big numbers in front of formulae, never the small numbers inside them. Count each element across the equation until both sides match.
low.analogy: Scaling a recipe: double the eggs by writing 2 eggs, never by pretending one egg holds two yolks — the item itself cannot change.
low.examPointer: Tally hydrogen and oxygen last; they usually meet in water on the product side and fall into place once the metals and groups are settled.

medium.restatement: A balanced symbol equation carries equal atom counts of every element on both sides; adjust the coefficients only, count an unchanged ion group such as nitrate as a single entity, and add state symbols where they are required.
medium.analogy: Bookkeeping with two columns: every element is an account, and each coefficient you write must debit one column and credit the other by exactly the same amount.
medium.examPointer: Changing a subscript — water H2O into hydrogen peroxide H2O2 — describes a different substance and scores zero, however neatly the equation then appears to balance.

check.stem: Which list names all the non-metals that must be written as molecules in symbol equations?

options.text: H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, I2
options.explanation: These seven non-metals exist as diatomic molecules and are written that way in equations.

options.text: H2, N2 and O2 only
options.explanation: The fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine molecules belong to the same set; three of the seven have been dropped.
options.misconception: recalls only the most familiar diatomic trio

options.text: H2, O2, N2, Cl2 and CO2
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a compound, not one of the elemental non-metals written as molecules.
options.misconception: slips a compound into the diatomic element list

options.text: Every element that is a gas at room temperature
options.explanation: The noble gases are gaseous elements yet exist as single atoms, so being a gas is not the test.
options.misconception: assumes every gaseous element is diatomic

check.stem: In a symbol equation, what does the state symbol (aq) mean?

options.text: Dissolved in water
options.explanation: (aq) marks an aqueous substance: one dissolved in water, as sodium hydroxide solution is in the neutralisation example.

options.text: A gas
options.explanation: A gas carries the symbol (g); (aq) is reserved for substances dissolved in water.
options.misconception: misreads (aq) as the gas state

options.text: A pure liquid
options.explanation: A pure liquid is (l); (aq) says the substance is spread through water, not melted into a pure liquid.
options.misconception: confuses aqueous with the pure liquid state

options.text: A solid
options.explanation: A solid is (s); (aq) belongs to substances dissolved in water.
options.misconception: misreads (aq) as the solid state

check.stem: The combustion of sulfur is written S (s) + O2 (g) → SO2 (g). What does this equation show?
check.misconceptionClass: reading particles from a symbol equation

options.text: One sulfur atom reacts with one oxygen molecule to make one sulfur dioxide molecule
options.explanation: S is single atoms, O2 is a molecule of two oxygen atoms, and the equation shows them combining one-to-one into SO2.

options.text: One sulfur molecule reacts with one oxygen molecule
options.explanation: Sulfur here is written as single atoms, not as molecules.
options.misconception: calls the sulfur atoms molecules

options.text: Two separate oxygen atoms react with the sulfur
options.explanation: The oxygen arrives as one O2 molecule; the equation does not split it into separate atoms.
options.misconception: splits the oxygen molecule into loose atoms

options.text: Sulfur dioxide forms as a liquid
options.explanation: The state symbol (g) after SO2 marks a gas.
options.misconception: ignores the state symbol on the product

check.stem: Al (s) + CuO (s) → Al2O3 (s) + Cu (s) needs balancing. Which balanced equation is correct?

options.text: 2Al (s) + 3CuO (s) → Al2O3 (s) + 3Cu (s)
options.explanation: Aluminium 2 = 2, oxygen 3 = 3 and copper 3 = 3, so every element tallies across the equation.

options.text: Al (s) + 3CuO (s) → Al2O3 (s) + 3Cu (s)
options.explanation: Only one aluminium atom is supplied on the left while Al2O3 needs two.
options.misconception: forgets to fix the aluminium count

options.text: 2Al (s) + 3CuO (s) → Al2O3 (s) + 2Cu (s)
options.explanation: The 3 CuO bring three copper atoms across, so the copper product must read 3Cu, not 2Cu.
options.misconception: leaves the copper tally unupdated

options.text: 2Al (s) + 2CuO (s) → Al2O3 (s) + 2Cu (s)
options.explanation: Two CuO supply only two oxygen atoms, but Al2O3 needs three; the oxygen tally is left short.
options.misconception: stops balancing before the oxygen tally closes

check.stem: An equation needs more oxygen on the product side. Why may you not balance it by changing H2O into H2O2?

options.text: H2O2 is a different substance, hydrogen peroxide, so the formula itself is fixed
options.explanation: Changing a small number inside a formula changes what the substance is; only the large numbers in front may be adjusted.

options.text: Subscripts may be changed freely, like coefficients
options.explanation: Coefficients scale the amount of a substance; subscripts redefine it. The two are not interchangeable.
options.misconception: treats subscripts as adjustable like coefficients

options.text: The hydrogen ratio would stay the same, so nothing changes
options.explanation: The hydrogen count is unchanged, but the oxygen count and the substance's identity both change, which is exactly the problem.
options.misconception: checks only one element and misses the identity change

options.text: Oxygen may never be added to the product side of an equation
options.explanation: Oxygen is added routinely by placing coefficients, such as writing O2 as a reactant; only formula edits are forbidden.
options.misconception: overgeneralises the ban into 'no oxygen may ever be added'

glossary.definition: The principle that nothing is lost or gained in a reaction; it is the basis of the Law of Conservation of Mass.
The law that the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products, because atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
A starting substance of a reaction, written on the left of the arrow.
A new substance formed in a reaction, written on the right of the arrow.
A substance added to make a reaction go faster; its name is written above the arrow when used.
The bracketed label (s), (l), (g) or (aq) that shows the physical state of each substance in a symbol equation.
Dissolved in water; shown with the state symbol (aq).
The number written in front of a formula to scale it while balancing; the formula itself may not be changed.

workedExample.prompt: All three worked examples from the note body, delineated: (1) build the word equation from a sentence — three cases, including one where the products are named first and one where burning in air supplies the missing reactant; (2) balance Al (s) + CuO (s) → Al2O3 (s) + Cu (s); (3) write the symbol equation for magnesium oxide reacting with nitric acid, forming magnesium nitrate and water.
steps: Example 1 — word equation from a sentence: ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate; the phrase to form marks where the arrow goes.
Example 1 — products named first: iron(II) hydroxide and sodium sulfate are formed, so they sit on the right: iron(II) sulfate + sodium hydroxide → iron(II) hydroxide + sodium sulfate.
Example 1 — detail partly missing: carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide; burning in air means oxygen is the second reactant.
Example 2 — aluminium first: the product Al2O3 carries 2 aluminium atoms, so 2 × 1 = 2 fixes the coefficient of Al.
Example 2 — oxygen next: 3 CuO supply the 3 oxygen atoms of Al2O3 and bring 3 × 1 = 3 copper atoms across, which fixes 3Cu.
Example 2 — balanced: 2Al (s) + 3CuO (s) → Al2O3 (s) + 3Cu (s); tally Al 2 = 2, O 3 = 3, Cu 3 = 3.
Example 3 — write the unbalanced equation from the sentence: MgO + HNO3 → Mg(NO3)2 + H2O; magnesium already matches.
Example 3 — balance hydrogen: the right side carries 2 hydrogen atoms, so 2 × 1 = 2 fixes 2 HNO3, and both nitrate groups settle with it.
Example 3 — final tally: each side holds 1 Mg, 2 H, 1 O outside the groups and 2 nitrate groups; balanced equation: MgO (s) + 2HNO3 (aq) → Mg(NO3)2 (aq) + H2O (l).
workedExample.finalAnswer: 2Al (s) + 3CuO (s) → Al2O3 (s) + 3Cu (s); MgO (s) + 2HNO3 (aq) → Mg(NO3)2 (aq) + H2O (l); word equations: ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate; iron(II) sulfate + sodium hydroxide → iron(II) hydroxide + sodium sulfate; carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide
